narrative: Your law school application was denied because the admissions model estimates a 91.7% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is a very high risk, and the committee determined that admitting you would likely set you up for failure. The largest reason for this prediction comes from your class rank. In both your first and third years, you placed in the bottom tenth of your class. By contrast, students who were accepted and later succeeded typically ranked around the middle of their class, roughly the sixth tenth. So from your first year onward, your standing was far below the level associated with passing the bar. The model sees this as the strongest signal that you would struggle, with your third-year rank counting more heavily than your first-year rank. Your family income bracket, while common among admitted students, also had a small influence and pointed in the same direction, though it was much less important than your academic performance. In other words, the decision was not driven by personal background but primarily by your record relative to your peers. If you want to pursue law, you need to address this core issue. Consider retaking challenging courses to improve your GPA, gaining work experience that demonstrates your ability to handle rigorous responsibilities, and retaking the LSAT to show a stronger aptitude. You may also want to seek schools where your profile fits better, but showing meaningful improvement in your academic standing will be essential.
